content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper studies how to effectively reuse a pretrained Transformer with a different vocabulary. It does so by investigating three different setups: a control one, a transfer to RoBERTa vocabulary and a cross-lingual one; through four different methods. Their results show that it is possible to warm-start this process but that some initializations are unstable.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
Strengths:
1. Interesting topic with clear execution and useful results
Weaknesses:
1. The authors claim that “Reinit Embed are sensitive to learning rates” but only test this hypothesis with two values (1e-4, 5e-4).
In the same sentence, the authors comment that “Reinit Embed are quite sensitive to the choice of which layers to update” while the experiments only investigate the extremes of this design (No layer updated, all layers updated)
2. The CLT experiments are only towards French and German, two languages that are very related to English. These are not enough nor representative for claims in CLT.
Questions:
1. What is DictMatch in FrankenBERTa? It is not obvious to me how Google Translate would be used there.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib: The paper has a good flow, from the motivation to the setup to the experiments. However, I found it hard, at first, to match experiments (Section4) with corresponding methods (Section2). Also, in the text, it is not clear when the Transformer layers are frozen and when not. Finally, the authors might want to better contextualise how FreqMatch differs from Gogoulou+ (2022) in Section2, as the current writing doesn’t make it clear to me what they mean by “explicit”.
content.summary_of_the_review: The paper investigates the interesting problem of repurposing language models to different vocabularies. The paper goes in-depth in a controlled study, which is, as such, not very applicable. On the other hand, it doesn’t consider the domain transfer setup where learning a related vocabulary might be important. Relatedly, the choice of languages used for cross-lingual transfer is suboptimal: more representative languages, across scripts and language families, would be required to make concrete suggestions in this setup.
content.correctness: 2: Several of the paper’s claims are incorrect or not well-supported.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 2: The contributions are only marginally significant or novel.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive feedback.

In response to (2), we performed preliminary experiments to arrive at this pair of learning rate settings and layer freezing/updating schemes, but felt that the inclusion of just the representative settings was adequate to support the analyses.

In response to (3), we acknowledge that the reviewer might prefer to see an analysis of the generalization behavior (or lack thereof) for the anchoring effect as the distance between the source and target languages grows, but we believe the analyses presented are still valuable in the English-German-French setting, and leave this set of extended experiments to future work. The goal of this paper was to understand how these initialization techniques impact the evolution of the word embedding distribution and geometry and how differently initialized models compare under these lenses as well as traditional evaluation metrics.

In response to (4), in the FrankenBERTa case, Dict Match does indeed simplify to an exact match between the two tokenizers, simply matching the words that occur in the vocabularies of both tokenizers despite the difference in underlying algorithms. 

On the “explicit” variant of Freq Match, in Section 2 of the updated pdf we have clarified the distinction between the original implementation in Gogoulou+ (2022) and the version we implemented in our evaluation.

Best,
Authors

content.confidence: 5: You are absolutely certain about your assessment. You are very familiar with the related work and checked the math/other details carefully.
content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper explores whether the vocabulary of a pretrained BERT model can be swapped posthoc by re-learning the embedding layer. The authors explore 3 settings (recovering some perturbed embeddings, transferring from WordPiece to BPE, and transferring from English to French/German) and 5 initialization schemes (randomly reinitializing the whole model or the embeddings, and reinitializing the embeddings based on frequency, alignment or dictionary matching). They conclude that swapping the vocabulary is indeed possible, and having a strong anchoring is important for best results.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
WEAKNESSES
- Very limited novelty (see below).
- Poorly positioned with respect to existing work in the area: most of the findings in the paper were already reported in the literature, but the narrative of the paper is not reflective of that.
- Multilingual experiments limited to only 2 high-resource and closely related languages (English to German/French).
- Some important experimental settings are unclear (see below).

STRENGTHS
- While the general findings are not new and the paper is poorly positioned with respect to it, there are some configurations that are new and have some interest (e.g. transferring from WordPiece to BPE).
- Even if the approach followed is rather simplistic, studying the geometry of the embeddings in addition to the downstream performance is new and complements the downstream results.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
There are some critical experimental details that are unclear. For instance, most prior work would finetune the model on the original vocabulary, and zero-shot transfer to the target vocabulary by plugging in its respective embeddings. From Figure 1, my understanding is that the authors are not doing this, and they instead finetune in the target language/vocabulary directly. However, the text is not clear at all, and all it says is that “we ground our embedding analysis to the real cross lingual transfer setting by quantifying the effectiveness of various initialization and training strategies using standard performance metrics”. If my understanding is correct, that would imply that the authors are finetuning on XNLI in German and French (which is also what Figure 1 is showing), but it is unclear how they would do that as the training set of XNLI is English-only. They might be using the official machine translated versions, but none of that is mentioned in the paper. These are not just minor implementation details, but a central part of the experimental setup. The omission of such details makes the results hard to reproduce and even interpret.

In addition to that, the main weakness of the paper is that the novelty is very limited. Artetxe et al. (ACL’20) already showed that it is possible to extend an English BERT model to a new language by learning a new embedding layer, just as this paper does, and Pfeiffer et al. (EMNLP’21) further studied the importance of initialization, which is the main dimension of analysis in this paper. There are several other papers studying the same setup, and Aji et al. (ACL’20) also compared different embedding initialization schemes in the context of NMT.

The authors cite some (although not all) of these papers, so they must be aware that most of their findings are not new. However, the paper is very poorly positioned in that respect, and things are presented as if they were novel when they are not. As someone that is familiar with this research topic, this made it irritating to read the paper and, for readers that are not familiar with it, the narrative would likely be misleading. This is clearly reflected in the introduction, which does not even cite any of the prior work studying the exact same problem, and follows a misleading narrative as exemplified by the following statements:

- “By contrast, little is known about swapping a vocabulary, which requires re-training the embedding layer of a model”: There are a few papers studying this exact same problem. You cannot pretend that they do not exist and claim that “little is known about swapping a vocabulary” without mentioning or citing any of them.

- “In this work, we ask whether it is possible to swap the vocabulary of a large language model after it has been trained”: This exact same question has already been answered positively in prior work.

- "Surprisingly, our observation carries over to this much harder learning problem - [...] adaptation of the model to a new language": This may have been surprising 2-3 years ago, but not anymore, as this exact same finding was presented in Artetxe et al. (ACL'20) and corroborated in subsequent work.
content.summary_of_the_review: I think that the paper does not meet the high bar of the conference and should thus be rejected. The primary issue is that the novelty is very limited and, to make things worse, the paper is very poorly positioned with respect to existing work in the area. Most of the findings in the paper were already reported in the literature, but the narrative of the paper is not reflective of that.

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive feedback.

To address the overall issues concerning the narrative and positioning of the paper, we have revised the second paragraph in the introduction to better contextualize the work and have also cited a few closely related papers that were previously only mentioned in the related works section. Further we have clearly spelled out a contributions list to describe the most important components of our analysis and evaluation.

To clarify the experimental details for the downstream task, XNLI, we have added the following line to the updated pdf:
>“For the downstream experiments on XNLI, we train and test in the target language, using the official machine translations provided.”

Finally, we would like to address themes common to the strengths cited by the reviewer as well as some of the specific statements with which they took issue through a clarification of our position. 

We designed two synthetic settings to accompany the traditional CLT experiments because we hypothesized that the embedding recovery and tokenization swapping case studies would facilitate a more thorough analysis of why the selection of initialization techniques we considered work as well as they do in the standard CLT setting despite the significant domain shift in the learning problem that swapping the tokenizer and embedding module of a transformer encoder represents. Our methodology produced evidence that an anchoring effect is exhibited to various degrees by each of the techniques from the literature, suggesting its mechanistic role. While we realize that there exists a body of work studying different forms of embedding swapping, and acknowledge that the reviewer might prefer to see an analysis of the generalization behavior (or lack thereof) for the anchoring effect as the distance between the source and target languages grows, we believe the analyses presented are still valuable in the English-German-French setting, and leave such a set of extended experiments to future work.

Best,
Authors

content.summary_of_the_paper: This paper investigates the ability to swap the token embedding of pre-trained language models without training from scratch. The main motivation is to adapt the model to different tokenizers (same or different languages). To achieve that the authors propose different initialization strategies and run experiments with swapping Roberta's embedding layer with that of BERT and re-purposing English BERT to French or German. The results show that the initialization is important and that it needs to be anchored to the original embedding.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
**Strengths**

Investigates different initialization strategies for successfully swapping the token embedding of a pre-trained model. 

Experiments show that it is possible to swap the token embeddings as long as they can be anchored sufficiently to the original token embedding.
 
**Weaknesses** 

Contributions and positioning with respect to prior work are not very clear; this is not the first paper to swap or re-learn the token embedding layer of a pre-trained model.  

The paper emphasizes the importance of using different vocabulary for special domains or different languages but the delivery is missing a use case where a successful change of token embedding leads to improvement (using the same model). 

Anchoring to original embedding is possible only when certain conditions about the original and the new vocabulary are met and it's not generally useful e.g. when tokens have no overlap, this hasn't been explored and discussed sufficiently. Overall, this reduces the scope of applicability in my view.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
Presentation, language, and formatting were generally good but the motivation and importance of contributions/results were not very clear. Positioning with respect to prior work and emphasis on what are the contributions and why they are important are lacking. 

The main idea and contributions have limited novelty; token embedding swapping has been previously attempted and the additional use cases presented here (FrankenBERTA) are not interesting enough (see below). Regarding the comparison of different initializations, there is not enough discussion to explain why this is non-obvious and what is the scope of applicability. There are several assumptions in the different initialization schemes that need to be made explicit in the introduction. 

Evaluation misses use cases that support the motivation and unique contributions claimed in this paper. 
- Learning a BERT token embedding using Roberta backbone is not surprising that works better than the original BERT (since Roberta is better trained) but worse than the original Roberta. A more interesting experiment would be to learn a token embedding that is suited for a special domain (e.g. technical terms) that performs better than the original token embedding.
- The cross-lingual results are below the language-specific models and there is no comparison to mBERT, so it's not clear what is the benefit exactly, especially given that Artetxe et al. (2020) have shown that swapping the token embedding from one language to another is competitive with mBERT. Is the initialization proposed in this work significantly better than the approach followed by Artetxe et al. (2020)? What are the differences?
content.summary_of_the_review: Overall, this paper focuses on an interesting problem but delivery requires more effort. The novel contributions of this work and the importance of results were not very clear. Emphasis on the novel aspects (e.g. comparison of initialization schemes), proper scoping, and presentation of more appealing use cases would make the study more convincing.

replying_to: Replying to Official Review of Paper5117 by Reviewer U9gg

content.title: Response
content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive feedback.

>“Contributions and positioning with respect to prior work are not very clear; this is not the first paper to swap or re-learn the token embedding layer of a pre-trained model,”

In the updated paper, we have added a clearly denoted contributions list in the introduction and have also cited a few closely related papers that were previously only mentioned in the related works section.

>“Anchoring to original embedding is possible only when certain conditions about the original and the new vocabulary are met and it's not generally useful e.g. when tokens have no overlap, this hasn't been explored and discussed sufficiently. Overall, this reduces the scope of applicability in my view.”

While we agree that there is an intuitive dependence on the relative _closeness_ of the source and target languages, we would like to draw attention to the fact that this family of techniques do not actually assume that matching pairs of tokens are present in the source and target vocabularies. The language in the comment “it’s not generally useful e.g. when tokens have no overlap” seems to presuppose that any of the techniques evaluated explicitly require this to be the case. Although it is most likely true that there needs to be some functional semantic overlap between a subset of the tokens in the vocabularies, in the case of natural language, we believe it is reasonable to assume that this exists, just to varying degrees. While we acknowledge that the reviewer might prefer to see an analysis of the generalization behavior (or lack thereof) for the anchoring effect as the distance between the source and target languages grows significantly, we believe the analyses presented are still valuable in the English-German-French setting.

Concerning the FrankenBERTa experiment, we believe that it is not unreasonable that a practitioner might build a pipeline that has preprocessed the dataset in one tokenizer but wants to use a stronger backbone model. Additionally, it is not so obvious (to the point of absolving any need for evidence) that the parameters of a pretrained transformer backbone model, RoBERTa in this case, paired with a Byte Pair Encoding based tokenizer, would be readily adaptable to a new tokenization algorithm such as WordPiece. We hypothesized that the success or failure of this second controlled vocabulary swap setting would shed light on the mechanisms behind and feasibility of the traditional CLT language swap setting.

In response to the comment about mBERT, we have included those results in the Appendix tables. When fine-tuning and testing mBERT on the same language, it noticeably underperforms its single-language counterparts on the high-resource languages we consider. It is worth noting that in our work we do not attempt to produce a multilingual model, and thus, benchmarking the techniques we consider against mBERT on this task would be an unfair comparison that would paint a skewed picture not directly relevant to our analyses. Finally, while it is true that Artetxe et al. (2020) reinitializes the entire embedding layer, an equivalent setting to the first initialization scheme we describe, ReinitEmbed, their work also focuses on creating a multilingual model from English BERT, rather than transforming English BERT into a monolingual model in a different language.

Best,
Authors

content.summary_of_the_paper: The paper explores the question of whether it is possible to swap out a model's vocabulary while retaining the original model's performance as much as possible. This covers both simple cases such as using a different tokeniser than what was originally used to train a model, as well as more complex cases such as doing a complete language swap. The authors propose various ways of initialising the new embedding matrix, in an attempt to transfer as much knowledge as possible from the initial embedding. They start by investigating whether a model whose embedding layer has been perturbed in various ways manages to recover it with training; they show that this is indeed possible by running a few studies with BERT. Then, they take a RoBERTa pretrained model and swap its vocabulary with that of BERT base; they show that the resulting model easily outperforms the original BERT base, and manages to retain most of RoBERTa's performance. Finally, they start with BERT base and swap out the English vocabulary for a French one, achieving (after fine-tuning) performance that is close to that of a model directly trained on French data.
content.strength_and_weaknesses:
## Strengths
* The problem that the authors try to address is clearly a very valuable one. One only has to think back to the beginning of the COVID-19 pandemic and how many NLP models were struggling to cope with the large amounts of new words that quickly entered our everyday vocabulary over the course of only a few weeks. More generally the idea of vocabulary swapping feels valuable within the field of crisis response, as well as for low-resource NLP.
* The writing is clear and easy to follow, and enough details are provided for readers to reimplement the described methods.
* The experimental setup feels reasonable and the performance of the resulting model, especially on the cross-lingual transfer experiments, is encouraging.


## Weaknesses
* The main point that surprised me is that this work is closely related to vocabulary substitution in neural machine translation, but the authors fail to compare or even discuss this in the paper. A discussion of how the proposed approach compares to the pre-existing literature is needed. Some key references:
  * Towards Continual Learning for Multilingual Machine Translation via Vocabulary Substitution: [Garcia et al. (2021)](https://aclanthology.org/2021.naacl-main.93.pdf)
  * The two papers by Lakew et al. mentioned here: <https://github.com/surafelml/adapt-mnmt>.
  * [Escolano et al. (2019)](https://aclanthology.org/P19-2033/)
* The link between the first experiment (embedding recovery) and the rest of the paper feels a bit weak to me. Could you help clarify how this experiment ties into the whole story, and how it helps answer the two hypotheses of section 2.3?
* While the language is clear, I found the structure of the paper hard to follow – the authors end up placing many central results in the Appendix, so readers are forced to jump back and forth. More on this below.

## Minor points
* The citation formats are the wrong way around – parenthetical citations are used where in-text citations should be used, and vice versa.
* In the definition of embedding correlation, a quick note on why average Pearson correlation was chosen instead of average cosine similarity would be good. (Shift invariance, I assume?)
* Typos:
  * Page 3, in the "Reinit Embed" paragraph: methods -> method
  * First sentence of section 2.3: is -> are
* Although it's obvious from context, from the legend of Figure 2 it's not clear which method corresponds to dash-dot-dot lines. The legend shows two dash-dot lines.
* The legends in most images are using a very small font.
content.clarity,_quality,_novelty_and_reproducib:
* The **Quality** of the experiments is generally good, with reasonable baselines and evaluation tasks. One important note, however, is that comparison to existing literature is somewhat lacking as it misses the whole area of vocabulary substitution in NMT.
* **Clarity** is generally good from the point of view of language. The structure would benefit from some significant work – the authors repeatedly reference material that feels central to the story but which is placed in the Appendix. This hurts readability, as readers will have to constantly ping-pong between the Appendix and the main paper to reference tables and figures. It also feels a bit unfair, as it allows the authors to add substantially more material than what would normally be allowed under the size limitations.
* In terms of **Originality**, the approach itself feels fairly simple, but the analysis is novel and insightful and the model is promising.
content.summary_of_the_review: A solid analysis of a fairly simple technique for vocabulary swapping that yields promising results, and which could have applications across several areas. The main weakness is in the lack of comparison to relevant related work in the field of MT.
content.correctness: 3: Some of the paper’s claims have minor issues. A few statements are not well-supported, or require small changes to be made correct.
content.technical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.
content.empirical_novelty_and_significance: 3: The contributions are significant and somewhat new. Aspects of the contributions exist in prior work.

content.comment:
Thank you for the constructive feedback.

In response to the suggested references, we have added these citations to the related works section and will include a more detailed discussion of connections to related work in MT in a future draft of the paper.

In response to comments on the structure of the figures and tables, we will improve the flow of the paper in terms of the figures, and the way in which appendix material is referenced, in a future draft of the paper.

For the following review comment: 
> “The link between the first experiment (embedding recovery) and the rest of the paper feels a bit weak to me. Could you help clarify how this experiment ties into the whole story, and how it helps answer the two hypotheses of section 2.3?”

We have included the following addition to Section 3.1 in the updated pdf:
> The value of a case study in recovering BERT embeddings derives from the controlled nature of the experimental setting. We suspect that the success of a cross lingual transfer under the traditional language swap scenario will be predicated on the feasibility of simply relearning a specific known embedding, under various levels of perturbation and different kinds of reinitialization.

Best, Authors
